body:
How nuclear energy produces electricity

Nuclear energy is the energy released when changes occur in the nucleus of an atom. Commercial nuclear power stations generate electricity through nuclear fission, in which a heavy atomic nucleus splits into smaller nuclei and releases a large amount of energy.

In a nuclear reactor, fission takes place as a controlled chain reaction. Neutrons released during one fission event can cause further fission events. The resulting heat is used to produce steam, which drives a turbine connected to an electrical generator. Thus, nuclear electricity is produced by converting nuclear energy into heat, mechanical energy and finally electrical energy.

Unlike a coal-fired power station, a nuclear power station does not obtain its heat by burning coal. However, nuclear fuel is a finite mineral resource, and the radioactive materials produced during reactor operation require careful management.

Fissile and fertile materials

Understanding India's nuclear programme begins with an important distinction between fissile and fertile materials.

Fissile material: A material whose nuclei can undergo fission after absorbing low-energy neutrons and can support a nuclear chain reaction under suitable conditions. Uranium-235, plutonium-239 and uranium-233 are important examples.

Fertile material: A material that is not ordinarily used to maintain a thermal-neutron fission chain reaction by itself but can absorb neutrons and eventually form a fissile isotope. Uranium-238 and thorium-232 are important examples.

Natural uranium contains approximately 0.7% uranium-235 and 99.3% uranium-238. The small uranium-235 fraction is fissile. Most of the remaining uranium consists of uranium-238, which is fertile and can eventually be converted into plutonium-239.

IsotopeBasic propertyImportance in India's programme
Uranium-235FissileSupports fission in natural-uranium reactors.
Uranium-238FertileCan be converted into plutonium-239.
Plutonium-239FissileProvides fuel for fast breeder reactors.
Thorium-232FertileCan be converted into uranium-233.
Uranium-233FissileForms the intended foundation of the thorium-based third stage.

Why India needs 3 stages

India has relatively limited domestic uranium resources compared with its large thorium resource potential. Uranium-bearing areas include the Singhbhum region of Jharkhand and parts of Rajasthan. Thorium occurs in minerals such as monazite found in coastal mineral sands, notably along parts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

Dr. Homi Jehangir Bhabha conceived India's nuclear programme around the long-term objective of using indigenous resources. The three-stage strategy aims first to generate electricity from natural uranium, then to produce and use plutonium in breeder reactors, and ultimately to make extensive use of thorium by converting it into uranium-233.

  1. Stage 1: Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors use natural uranium and provide plutonium-bearing spent fuel for recovery.
  2. Stage 2: Fast Breeder Reactors use plutonium-based fuel and breed additional fissile material.
  3. Stage 3: Thorium-based systems are intended to use uranium-233 produced from thorium-232.

The stages are linked through their fuel materials. They are not simply 3 successive designs of the same reactor, and they do not imply that every nuclear power station in India belongs to one of the 3 stages.

Prelims focus

  • Homi J. Bhabha conceived India's nuclear programme.
  • Natural uranium contains approximately 0.7% uranium-235 and 99.3% uranium-238.
  • Uranium-235, plutonium-239 and uranium-233 are fissile materials.
  • Uranium-238 and thorium-232 are fertile materials.
  • Monazite-bearing coastal sands are an important source of thorium in India.
  • Trap: Thorium-232 is fertile, not a material that can independently sustain the intended thermal-neutron chain reaction.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, chapter Structure of the Atom, printed pp. 52–53; NCERT, Science, Class 10, chapter Sources of Energy, section 14.3.4, printed pp. 251–252, 2021–22 printing; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, printed pp. 34–35, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter Mineral and Energy Resources, printed pp. 80–82; Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, About Us, section Atomic Energy in India, consulted 15 November 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Nuclear Power Programme, 23 July 2026.]

title: Why India Developed a Three-Stage Nuclear Power Programme

body:
The first stage begins with natural uranium

The first stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme is based mainly on Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs). These reactors can use natural uranium as fuel without first increasing its uranium-235 concentration through enrichment.

The fuel is generally natural uranium dioxide. Its uranium-235 component undergoes fission and releases heat. At the same time, some uranium-238 nuclei absorb neutrons and are converted through nuclear processes into plutonium-239. This creates a connection between electricity production in Stage 1 and fuel availability for Stage 2.

Why heavy water is important

Ordinary water contains hydrogen, whereas heavy water contains deuterium, a heavier isotope of hydrogen. Its chemical formula is D2O.

In an Indian PHWR, heavy water serves 2 important purposes:

  • Moderator: It slows down neutrons released during fission. Slower neutrons are more likely to induce fission in uranium-235, helping sustain a controlled chain reaction using natural uranium.
  • Primary coolant: It carries heat away from the reactor fuel. That heat is subsequently used to produce steam for electricity generation.

Heavy water is useful because it slows neutrons while absorbing relatively few of them. This helps a PHWR make effective use of the small uranium-235 fraction present in natural uranium.

Heavy water is neither the nuclear fuel nor a source of energy by itself. Uranium is the fuel; heavy water helps the reactor sustain the reaction and transfer heat.

How a PHWR produces electricity

  1. Fission of uranium-235 releases heat and neutrons in the reactor fuel.
  2. Heavy water moderates neutrons and carries heat from the fuel.
  3. Heat is transferred to water that produces steam.
  4. Steam drives a turbine connected to a generator, producing electricity.
  5. After use, the reactor fuel contains unused uranium, newly produced plutonium and radioactive fission products.

The energy-production process resembles other steam-turbine power stations at its final stage. The important difference lies in the source of heat: controlled nuclear fission rather than combustion.

Why spent fuel matters to the next stage

Spent fuel is nuclear fuel that has been removed from a reactor after irradiation. It is not simply material with no remaining useful substances. It contains residual uranium, plutonium formed during operation and radioactive fission products.

Under the controlled processes of the nuclear fuel cycle, usable uranium and plutonium can be recovered from spent fuel through reprocessing. The recovered plutonium is important because it provides fissile material for fast breeder reactors in Stage 2. Radioactive waste that cannot be reused must be managed and stored appropriately.

This is why the first stage has 2 strategic functions: producing electricity and developing a source of fissile material for the next stage.

PHWR and PWR are different reactor types

A PHWR uses heavy water as its moderator and primary coolant and can use natural uranium fuel. A conventional Pressurised Water Reactor (PWR) uses ordinary light water and typically uses enriched uranium fuel. The names sound similar, but heavy water and light water are not interchangeable terms.

This distinction becomes important when identifying Indian nuclear power stations. Kakrapar and Kaiga have PHWR units, while Kudankulam uses PWR technology.

Prelims focus

  • Stage 1 is based mainly on Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors.
  • Indian PHWRs use natural uranium dioxide as fuel.
  • Heavy water has the formula D2O.
  • Heavy water acts as both moderator and primary coolant in Indian PHWRs.
  • Plutonium-239 formed from uranium-238 can be recovered from spent PHWR fuel for Stage 2.
  • Trap: PHWR and PWR are not the same reactor type.

[Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, About Us, section Atomic Energy in India, consulted 15 November 2026; Nuclear Fuel Complex, Nuclear Power Station, consulted 15 November 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Nuclear Fuel Programme, 23 July 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 10, chapter Sources of Energy, section 14.3.4, printed pp. 251–252, 2021–22 printing.]

title: Stage 1: Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors and Natural Uranium

body:
From recovered plutonium to new reactor fuel

The second stage of India's nuclear programme uses Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs). These reactors are intended to make better use of uranium resources by using plutonium-based fuel and converting additional fertile material into fissile material.

Plutonium-239 recovered from Stage 1 spent fuel provides an important starting fissile material. Unlike a PHWR, which uses slowed-down or thermal neutrons, a fast reactor operates mainly with fast neutrons. The neutrons are not deliberately slowed by a moderator in the way they are in a PHWR.

What does breeding mean?

A breeder reactor is designed to produce fissile material from fertile material. In India's second-stage strategy, uranium-238 is an important fertile material. When it captures neutrons, it can eventually be converted into plutonium-239.

A fast breeder reactor uses fissile material to maintain its fission chain reaction. Fertile material around the fuel can also absorb neutrons and form additional fissile material. A breeder is designed so that, over its fuel cycle, it can produce more fissile material than it consumes.

Breeding does not create energy or fuel from nothing. It converts an existing fertile material into a fissile material by using neutrons produced during reactor operation.

The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam

India's major second-stage project is the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu.

The PFBR uses mixed oxide (MOX) fuel containing uranium and plutonium. Its fuel region is surrounded by a blanket containing uranium-238. Neutrons from the reactor can convert uranium-238 in this blanket into plutonium-239. This is the central breeding principle relevant to the second stage.

The PFBR is a sodium-cooled fast reactor. Sodium serves as a coolant, while the reactor's fission process relies on fast neutrons rather than a heavy-water moderator. For prelims preparation, the essential distinction is between fast-neutron breeding in the PFBR and moderated-neutron fission in a PHWR.

IGCAR and BHAVINI have different roles

The Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) developed the indigenous technology and design of the PFBR.

Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), a public sector undertaking under the Department of Atomic Energy, is responsible for building and commissioning the PFBR.

Both institutions are connected with Kalpakkam, but their roles should not be confused: IGCAR is the principal research and design institution, whereas BHAVINI is the company undertaking the PFBR project.

What happened in 2026?

The PFBR achieved first criticality on 6 April 2026. First criticality means that the reactor achieved a controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction for the first time. It is a major scientific and commissioning milestone.

However, first criticality is not the same as commercial electricity generation. After achieving criticality, a reactor must undergo additional testing, controlled power increases, regulatory clearances and other commissioning activities before regular commercial operation.

In its official update dated 29 July 2026, the Department of Atomic Energy stated that BHAVINI was commissioning the PFBR and that full commissioning was expected by March 2027. This was a projected completion date, not a confirmed date of commercial operation. The dates and status here are based on official updates available for the lesson cutoff of 15 November 2026.

How Stage 2 prepares for Stage 3

Fast breeder reactors are also central to the planned use of thorium. A future breeding arrangement can use thorium-232 to produce uranium-233, which is the intended fissile material for the third stage.

It is important to distinguish the present PFBR fuel arrangement from the long-term plan. The PFBR's uranium-plutonium MOX fuel and uranium-238 blanket are part of its described initial configuration. The use of thorium in a breeder blanket is a planned route towards the third stage, not evidence that commercial thorium-based power generation has already begun.

Prelims focus

  • Stage 2 uses Fast Breeder Reactors.
  • India's PFBR is located at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu and has a rated electrical capacity of 500 MWe.
  • PFBR fuel is uranium-plutonium mixed oxide.
  • Uranium-238 in the breeder blanket can be converted into plutonium-239.
  • IGCAR developed the PFBR design; BHAVINI undertakes the project.
  • PFBR achieved first criticality on 6 April 2026.
  • Trap: First criticality does not mean that commercial operation has started.

[Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, About Us, section Atomic Energy in India, consulted 15 November 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu Attains First Criticality, 7 April 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Operational Performance of NPCIL Nuclear Power Plants, 29 July 2026; Department of Atomic Energy, Parliamentary Question: Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor, 5 August 2026.]
